newsitem.title: SWEDEN: ANALYSTS SCEPTICAL OVER SWEDISH PULP PRICE RISE.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS SCEPTICAL OVER SWEDISH PULP PRICE RISE.

text.p: Swedish forestry companies may find it hard to implement announced pulp price increases to 610 million a tonne from 560 with support for the rise not universal, several forestry analysts said on Wednesday.
"I do not think this (price hike) will be implemented," said Erik Magnusson, analyst at Nordbanken .
"It is too early in the season...(as) demand for fine paper is low in January/February. Conditions should be better in March/April."

North American Scandinavian (Norscan) pulp inventories are also rather high although they might have fallen slightly, according to Sherman Chao at Merrill Lynch in New York, who was surprised by the announced price increases.
"You can ask yourself what the purpose of the (price increase) announcements really is," he said.
"I can think of three reasons: that companies really believe in improved market conditions, (that they want) to stabilise operations or to confuse 'the enemy'."
A spokesman for the U.S.'s Weyerhaeuser , the world's largest producer of pulp, told Reuters in New York that the company does not comment on its planned price hikes as it informs customers first.
But one analyst said he had recently spoken to Weyerhaeuser's president and the U.S. group doubted a pulp price increase would come to fruition in the near future.
Chao at Merrill Lynch doubted that Swedish forestry companies could see through their price increases if Weyerhaeuser did not go along with them.
"It will probably be very hard for them to get acceptance for their price hikes if they are not accompanied by the world's largest producer," Chao said.
"But you have to remember that Weyerhaeuser's list price on long-fibre pulp is at 620 a tonne and I have a feeling that spot prices are not that for off."
Swedish forestry group Sodra agreed that Weyerhaeuser's view is important.

"It will be hard to increase prices without Weyerhaeuser's support," head of marketing Hans Burmeister said. "On the other hand, I had not expected to hear from Weyerhaeuser yet. They are rather sensitive about reacting too quickly on competitors' price changes, not wanting to get on the wrong side of competition authorities."
Both Chao and Burmeister said the market's focus on Norscan was not sound as the inventories do not reflect the true sector situation.
"It is possible that inventories are falling somewhat," Chao said, but pointed to large production cutbacks in the U.S. and Canada in recent months.
Burmeister said that actual deliveries constitute a better indicator than Norscan as inventories have followed certain patterns over the cycles.
